frictionVectors.title: EU GAS DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Algeria retains strong state control over hydrocarbons, but European export markets, pipeline links and LNG infrastructure give external buyers leverage over future investment and pricing.

frictionVectors.title: SAHEL SECURITY SPILLOVER
frictionVectors.details: Instability across Mali, Niger and Libya increases border-security costs and complicates Algiers's effort to preserve regional autonomy without relying on foreign military actors.

frictionVectors.title: OIL INFRASTRUCTURE CONCENTRATION
frictionVectors.details: Angola controls its petroleum sector institutionally, but dependence on offshore oil, foreign operators and export infrastructure leaves national revenue exposed to external technology, capital and price cycles.

frictionVectors.title: DEBT AND CORRIDOR LEVERAGE
frictionVectors.details: Chinese lending and major infrastructure relationships remain strategically important, while the Lobito Corridor attracts competing Western and Gulf interest around minerals and logistics.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND LOGISTICS DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Cotonou is central to Benin's economic sovereignty, but trade flows, port modernization and regional connectivity depend heavily on foreign contractors, finance and relations with Nigeria.

frictionVectors.title: NORTHERN SECURITY FRONTIER
frictionVectors.details: Jihadist activity and cross-border insecurity near Burkina Faso and Niger threaten transport corridors, agricultural zones and the state's ability to control northern resources.

frictionVectors.title: DIAMOND MARKET CONCENTRATION
frictionVectors.details: Botswana exercises comparatively strong oversight through state-linked diamond institutions, but remains exposed to global demand, De Beers-linked arrangements and external processing capacity.

frictionVectors.title: NEW MINERALS, NEW LEVERAGE
frictionVectors.details: Efforts to develop copper, nickel, lithium and other minerals require foreign capital and technical expertise, creating a sovereignty trade-off despite strong domestic institutions.

frictionVectors.title: ARTISANAL GOLD AND ILLICIT FLOWS
frictionVectors.details: Gold is central to the government's sovereignty narrative, but artisanal production, smuggling and insecurity limit fiscal capture and create openings for foreign intermediaries.

frictionVectors.title: RUSSIAN SECURITY DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: The shift away from Western security partnerships toward Russian support may increase regime autonomy in the short term, but it risks opaque resource-security bargains and reduced infrastructure financing options.

highlights: Nickel and rare-earth ambitions attract foreign capital
Regional tensions constrain trade and security space

frictionVectors.title: MINING CONCESSION DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Burundi is seeking investment to develop nickel and other mineral deposits, but limited state capacity risks weak revenue capture and opaque concession terms.

frictionVectors.title: RWANDA BORDER FRICTION
frictionVectors.details: Political and security tensions with Rwanda disrupt cross-border commerce and complicate regional infrastructure and mineral-export routes.

highlights: Tourism and external finance remain structural dependencies

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND DIGITAL INFRASTRUCTURE COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: Cabo Verde is balancing European, Chinese, and other foreign partners around ports, connectivity, and digital infrastructure while seeking to preserve strategic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: TOURISM-LED RESOURCE PRESSURE
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-owned tourism and real-estate investment supports growth but increases exposure to external demand, land pressures, and water scarcity.

highlights: Oil, gas, and mining remain externally financed
Conflict zones weaken national control of infrastructure

frictionVectors.title: RESOURCE-SECTOR REVENUE LEAKAGE
frictionVectors.details: Foreign firms remain central to hydrocarbons, mining, and major infrastructure, limiting domestic value capture despite the state's formal ownership of resources.

frictionVectors.title: ANGLOPHONE AND FAR-NORTH INSECURITY
frictionVectors.details: Separatist violence in the Northwest and Southwest and militant threats in the Far North disrupt roads, trade corridors, and public-service delivery.

highlights: Russian security backing expands political leverage
Gold and diamond networks remain weakly governed

frictionVectors.title: RUSSIAN SECURITY-RESOURCE NEXUS
frictionVectors.details: Russian security personnel and associated commercial interests retain influence around regime protection and mining, raising concerns over opaque access to gold and diamonds.

frictionVectors.title: CORRIDOR AND MINING INSECURITY
frictionVectors.details: Armed-group activity and fragile transport links limit state oversight of extraction and keep dependence on neighboring countries for trade routes and fuel.

highlights: Oil revenues still anchor state sovereignty
Security realignment widens external bargaining space

frictionVectors.title: OIL TRANSIT AND REVENUE DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Chad's fiscal position remains tightly tied to oil production and export infrastructure, leaving the state vulnerable to foreign operators, pipeline constraints, and price volatility.

frictionVectors.title: POST-FRENCH SECURITY COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: The drawdown of French military involvement creates room for expanded Russian, Gulf, and regional engagement while complicating the country's security guarantees and strategic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: France and Mayotte
frictionVectors.details: France retains control of Mayotte, making sovereignty and maritime-boundary claims a persistent diplomatic fault line. Comoros has limited leverage beyond international advocacy and regional diplomacy.

frictionVectors.title: Maritime Resource Constraints
frictionVectors.details: Weak surveillance capacity leaves fisheries and maritime resources vulnerable to foreign exploitation. External financing and remittances support stability but do not substantially expand sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: M23 and Rwanda Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Conflict involving M23 and alleged external backing continues to undermine Kinshasa's territorial control in the east. Regional mediation and security partnerships have produced limited durable enforcement.

frictionVectors.title: Cobalt and Copper Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Chinese firms remain deeply embedded in mining and processing, while the United States and Europe seek alternative critical-mineral access. The state is gaining bargaining power but still captures too little value relative to the scale of extraction.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Public finances and export earnings remain heavily exposed to offshore oil and volatile prices. Limited diversification weakens the state's capacity to convert resource wealth into broad sovereign resilience.

frictionVectors.title: External Infrastructure Finance
frictionVectors.details: Chinese and other foreign-backed infrastructure relationships provide essential roads, ports, and urban projects while increasing dependence on external capital. Debt and contract transparency remain recurring sovereignty concerns.

frictionVectors.title: Cocoa Processing and Foreign Buyers
frictionVectors.details: Côte d'Ivoire is expanding local processing and state oversight, but multinational traders and external price conditions still capture significant value. Climate stress and farmer incomes remain major vulnerabilities.

frictionVectors.title: French and Gulf Competition
frictionVectors.details: France remains influential in finance, security, and business, while Gulf and other investors are expanding around ports, logistics, and infrastructure. Abidjan benefits from competition but must manage strategic dependence.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Military Bases
frictionVectors.details: US, Chinese, French, Japanese, and other military presences generate revenue and deterrence but constrain strategic autonomy. Competition among external powers raises Djibouti's leverage while increasing exposure to regional crises.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and Port Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-financed infrastructure and the Doraleh-centered logistics economy remain central to growth, with debt and concession terms limiting policy flexibility. Dependence on Ethiopian trade and Red Sea traffic adds further vulnerability.

frictionVectors.title: GERD and Nile security
frictionVectors.details: Egypt continues to oppose unilateral Ethiopian control over Nile flows and seeks a binding operating framework for the GERD. The dispute remains tightly linked to regional diplomacy and water security.

frictionVectors.title: External financing and strategic assets
frictionVectors.details: IMF requirements and Gulf investment provide liquidity but increase outside influence over major land, port, and infrastructure assets. Cairo is balancing urgent financing needs against preserving state control.

frictionVectors.title: Maturing oil and gas fields
frictionVectors.details: Falling production is tightening fiscal space and increasing pressure to attract foreign operators and gas-processing investment. The state remains formally dominant, but reduced resource revenues weaken bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: External infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chinese financing and construction remain important for ports, roads, and public facilities. Debt and project concentration limit diversification of external partnerships.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea militarization
frictionVectors.details: Eritrea's coastline and proximity to shipping routes attract competing regional and extra-regional interest. As maritime insecurity persists, outside powers may seek access while Asmara resists formal alignment.

frictionVectors.title: Mining sovereignty and sanctions risk
frictionVectors.details: The government tightly controls major mining activity and limits transparency, creating recurring friction with foreign investors and rights monitors. Revenue concentration leaves the sector vulnerable to commodity and diplomatic shocks.

frictionVectors.title: Regional economic dependence
frictionVectors.details: Eswatini relies heavily on South African trade corridors, electricity links, finance, and the SACU revenue pool. This interdependence constrains independent resource and industrial policy.

frictionVectors.title: Trade-preference exposure
frictionVectors.details: Textile and sugar industries remain sensitive to external market access and changing preference regimes, especially in the United States and regional blocs. Any disruption would quickly affect employment and foreign exchange.

frictionVectors.title: Nile and Red Sea contest
frictionVectors.details: Ethiopia is using the GERD and its search for maritime access to expand strategic autonomy, but both moves intensify friction with Egypt, Sudan, and Somalia. External mediation and Gulf involvement remain significant.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring, IMF engagement, and reliance on foreign contractors constrain Addis Ababa's control over major infrastructure and foreign-exchange policy. Conflict-related reconstruction further increases dependence on external finance.

highlights: Oil and manganese remain externally tied

frictionVectors.title: Resource-sector renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The transitional authorities are seeking greater state control and domestic value addition in oil, manganese and timber. Renegotiation risks friction with established foreign operators and financiers.

frictionVectors.title: France and regional balancing
frictionVectors.details: Libreville is diversifying diplomatic and commercial ties beyond France while managing dependence on established French-linked networks and regional security partners.

highlights: Fisheries and energy sovereignty under pressure

frictionVectors.title: Senegal-linked infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Gambia relies heavily on Senegal for regional transport, electricity interconnection and security cooperation. This improves resilience but limits independent strategic leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign fishing access
frictionVectors.details: Industrial fishing by foreign fleets continues to generate concerns over depleted stocks, weak monitoring and limited local benefits. Fisheries governance is a recurring sovereignty issue.

highlights: Gold and critical minerals face governance stress

frictionVectors.title: Gold and illegal mining
frictionVectors.details: Galamsey damages water systems and agricultural land while exposing gaps in state enforcement and illicit trading networks. Foreign-linked equipment and buyers complicate efforts to retain value domestically.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and infrastructure leverage
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and IMF-supported reforms constrain fiscal autonomy, while Chinese and other external lenders remain important for infrastructure and commodities-related financing.

frictionVectors.title: Simandou concession competition
frictionVectors.details: The iron-ore corridor is attracting major Chinese and other foreign capital, creating opportunities for state revenue but also risks of enclave development, opaque contracting and external leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Junta control over mining
frictionVectors.details: The military government is using licensing reviews and local-content demands to strengthen control over bauxite and iron ore. Political restrictions and uncertain transition timelines raise investor and regional tensions.

highlights: Fragile institutions shield a cashew economy

frictionVectors.title: Cashew-chain dependency
frictionVectors.details: The economy remains highly dependent on raw cashew exports, leaving producers vulnerable to foreign buyers, price swings and limited domestic processing capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Maritime and narcotics exposure
frictionVectors.details: Weak naval and judicial capacity leaves coastal waters exposed to illegal fishing and transnational trafficking. External security assistance is necessary but reinforces limited sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: External Debt Exposure
frictionVectors.details: IMF-linked fiscal reforms and large obligations to China and private creditors constrain Nairobi's policy autonomy. Debt-service demands continue to compete with infrastructure and social spending.

frictionVectors.title: Mombasa Corridor Competition
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed rail, port, and logistics projects remain central to Kenya's trade strategy but raise concerns over commercial control and long-term revenue capture.

frictionVectors.title: Highlands Water Transfers
frictionVectors.details: Lesotho's water exports to South Africa provide essential revenue but deepen dependence on a larger neighbor and expose the kingdom to disputes over pricing, project delays, and benefit distribution.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Owned Manufacturing
frictionVectors.details: The textile and apparel sector relies heavily on external investors and preferential market access, leaving employment and export earnings vulnerable to shifts in United States and regional trade policy.

frictionVectors.title: Iron Ore and Resource Concessions
frictionVectors.details: Large foreign mining and logistics interests are reviving exports, but contract transparency, local procurement, and revenue-sharing remain central sovereignty concerns.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Road Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Liberia depends on external finance and operators for major transport infrastructure, limiting domestic control over strategic corridors while offering opportunities to renegotiate terms.

frictionVectors.title: Oil Infrastructure Rivalry
frictionVectors.details: Competing political and armed authorities continue to use oil fields, terminals, and the national budget as leverage. Foreign commercial and political patrons amplify disputes over production and revenue allocation.

frictionVectors.title: Mercenary and Base Presence
frictionVectors.details: External military, intelligence, and security networks retain influence around strategic territory and energy infrastructure, weakening unified Libyan control over national security decisions.

frictionVectors.title: Nickel and Cobalt Concessions
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-led mining projects provide export earnings and infrastructure but leave Madagascar exposed to commodity cycles, environmental damage, and disputes over tax and community benefits.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Energy Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Weak domestic power and transport networks increase reliance on foreign financiers and operators, reducing the state's bargaining power over strategic mineral supply chains.

frictionVectors.title: IMF-LED FISCAL CONDITIONALITY
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and external financing requirements limit Malawi's room to direct public investment and control strategic assets. Currency and fuel shortages amplify dependence on donors and lenders.

frictionVectors.title: MINING AND POWER BOTTLENECKS
frictionVectors.details: Foreign participation in uranium, rare-earth, and other mineral projects is rising while unreliable electricity and transport infrastructure restrict domestic value capture.

frictionVectors.title: GOLD NATIONALIZATION PRESSURE
frictionVectors.details: Bamako is seeking a larger state share and tighter regulation of industrial mining, raising tensions with foreign operators and investors. Informal extraction and opaque contracting continue to weaken revenue capture.

frictionVectors.title: RUSSIAN SECURITY DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Reliance on Russian-linked security forces expands Moscow's influence over security and political decision-making. Persistent jihadist violence exposes the limits of this partnership and disrupts mining corridors.

frictionVectors.title: GTA GAS DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: The Greater Tortue Ahmeyim gas development with Senegal brings revenue and geopolitical leverage but leaves Mauritania dependent on foreign operators, shared infrastructure, and cross-border coordination.

frictionVectors.title: MINING CORRIDOR CONTROL
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-led iron-ore and prospective green-hydrogen projects require major ports, rail, and power investment. Weak domestic processing capacity risks retaining an export-oriented, low-value structure.

frictionVectors.title: CHAGOS SOVEREIGNTY NEGOTIATIONS
frictionVectors.details: The Chagos dispute remains central to Mauritius's territorial sovereignty and maritime-resource claims. Any settlement involving the Diego Garcia military facility must balance national control with British and United States strategic interests.

frictionVectors.title: OFFSHORE FINANCE PRESSURE
frictionVectors.details: International tax-transparency and anti-money-laundering standards constrain Mauritius's offshore financial model. Compliance pressure could reduce external leverage while also limiting a major source of services revenue.

frictionVectors.title: WESTERN SAHARA RESOURCE CONTEST
frictionVectors.details: Morocco's control and development of Western Sahara supports its strategic resource and infrastructure agenda but remains contested by the Polisario Front and subject to legal and diplomatic scrutiny.

frictionVectors.title: EXTERNAL CAPITAL DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: European, Gulf, Chinese, and United States investment is accelerating ports, renewables, automotive, and defense-linked infrastructure. Rabat retains strong bargaining power, but external financing and technology remain important inputs.

highlights: LNG restart remains hostage to Cabo Delgado security
Resource wealth is expanding faster than local control

frictionVectors.title: Cabo Delgado LNG Security
frictionVectors.details: Insurgent violence continues to constrain the offshore LNG megaproject and sustain dependence on foreign security support. Any restart will intensify disputes over revenue sharing, local employment, and provincial autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: External Energy Leverage
frictionVectors.details: International energy firms and lenders retain substantial influence over project timing, financing, and revenue structures. Maputo is seeking greater domestic benefit while managing fiscal pressure and investor confidence.

highlights: Critical-mineral and oil ambitions attract competing partners
Wind, hydrogen, and uranium strategy tests state capacity

frictionVectors.title: Green Hydrogen and Port Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed hydrogen projects could diversify the economy but may leave Namibia dependent on external capital, export markets, and infrastructure operators. Local-content and water-use concerns are becoming central sovereignty issues.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Oil Governance
frictionVectors.details: Recent offshore discoveries have raised expectations while licensing and development decisions remain closely tied to multinational operators. The government faces pressure to establish credible fiscal, environmental, and community-benefit rules before production.

highlights: Junta consolidates control over uranium and oil assets

frictionVectors.title: Uranium and Mining Renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The military government is challenging legacy arrangements with foreign miners and asserting greater control over strategic resources. Production and investment face uncertainty as Niamey balances sovereignty claims against technical and market dependence.

frictionVectors.title: Security Partnership Shift
frictionVectors.details: The withdrawal of Western forces and closer ties with Russia and Sahel partners have altered intelligence, logistics, and counterinsurgency access. Insurgent activity remains a major constraint on transport corridors and resource development.

highlights: Oil-sector reform collides with production insecurity
Gas and refining infrastructure reshape energy sovereignty

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline Theft and Niger Delta Control
frictionVectors.details: Crude theft, sabotage, and community conflict continue to reduce output and weaken federal control over production corridors. International oil companies are balancing divestment, security costs, and pressure to retain strategic assets.

frictionVectors.title: Refining and Foreign Capital
frictionVectors.details: New domestic refining capacity could reduce import dependence, but financing, feedstock access, and market concentration create new leverage points for private and foreign-linked actors. Gas infrastructure remains vulnerable to underinvestment and regional insecurity.

highlights: Security influence expands alongside regional diplomatic costs
Mineral supply chains remain exposed to DRC tensions

frictionVectors.title: Eastern DRC Conflict
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda's alleged support for the M23 rebellion remains a major source of regional confrontation and international pressure. Cross-border insecurity affects trade routes, diplomatic relations, and perceptions of Rwanda's role in critical-mineral networks.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic External Partnerships
frictionVectors.details: Security, technology, and development partnerships provide Kigali with substantial state capacity and diplomatic leverage. They also increase scrutiny over accountability, political space, and the distribution of benefits from regional mineral and logistics networks.

frictionVectors.title: OFFSHORE EXPLORATION UNCERTAINTY
frictionVectors.details: Exploration in the Gulf of Guinea offers potential revenue but has yet to deliver a commercial petroleum sector. Limited state capacity increases dependence on foreign operators and technical partners.

frictionVectors.title: MARITIME SECURITY DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: São Tomé and Príncipe relies on external partners, including Portugal and Gulf of Guinea security initiatives, to monitor its waters and protect prospective offshore assets.

frictionVectors.title: OIL AND GAS CONTRACT RENEGOTIATION
frictionVectors.details: The government is pressing for greater national control and fiscal returns from the Sangomar and Greater Tortue Ahmeyim projects. Tensions with international operators and lenders could affect investment confidence and project expansion.

frictionVectors.title: DEBT AND INFRASTRUCTURE PRESSURE
frictionVectors.details: Debt constraints limit Dakar's room to finance ports, power, and transport independently. External creditors and infrastructure contractors retain substantial leverage over the timing and terms of development.

frictionVectors.title: FISHERIES ACCESS AND CONTROL
frictionVectors.details: Foreign fishing fleets and external fisheries agreements continue to test Seychelles' ability to capture value from its maritime zone. Monitoring capacity remains a core sovereignty constraint.

frictionVectors.title: INDIAN OCEAN STRATEGIC COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles balances security and infrastructure ties with India, China, Gulf states, and Western partners. Port, surveillance, and maritime-security cooperation can generate political sensitivity over strategic dependence.

frictionVectors.title: MINING CONCESSION DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore, rutile, bauxite, and gold projects remain dominated by foreign capital and operators, limiting domestic control over pricing, logistics, and downstream processing. Revenue volatility leaves the state vulnerable to commodity-cycle shocks.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND CORRIDOR LEVERAGE
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed port, road, and mining-corridor projects can improve connectivity but may lock the government into asymmetric financing and concession terms. Competition among Chinese, Gulf, and Western interests increases bargaining pressure.

frictionVectors.title: EXTERNAL SECURITY DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Somalia's federal government remains reliant on international forces, Turkey, Gulf partners, and donor-backed institutions for security and state infrastructure. Divergent external relationships can complicate federal authority and maritime policy.

frictionVectors.title: MARITIME RIGHTS AND OFFSHORE OIL
frictionVectors.details: Offshore petroleum prospects and contested maritime interests are drawing foreign commercial and political attention before Somalia has fully secured regulatory and security capacity. Weak enforcement raises the risk of unequal contracts and disputes over federal and regional jurisdiction.

highlights: Power and rail constraints erode leverage

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals influence
frictionVectors.details: The United States, China, and European partners are competing for access to platinum-group metals, manganese, and other strategic minerals. South Africa retains formal sovereignty but faces pressure to align supply chains with external blocs.

frictionVectors.title: Electricity and freight bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: Grid instability and deteriorating rail and port infrastructure weaken the state’s ability to capture value from mining and exports. Private and foreign capital is increasingly positioned to fill infrastructure gaps.

highlights: Oil remains the state’s fiscal lifeline

frictionVectors.title: Oil corridor vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan depends on Sudanese export infrastructure, leaving its principal revenue stream exposed to war, sabotage, and bargaining by neighboring authorities. Foreign oil operators retain substantial technical and commercial influence.

frictionVectors.title: Elite-controlled resource access
frictionVectors.details: Political fragmentation and insecurity allow armed and political networks to divert oil revenues and control local trade routes. Weak institutions limit the state’s ability to convert resource ownership into broad-based development.

highlights: War fragments control of gold and transit routes
Red Sea access becomes strategic prize

frictionVectors.title: Gold and war economies
frictionVectors.details: Competing armed actors and foreign-linked trading networks exploit gold production and export channels to finance the conflict. Sovereign oversight is severely degraded across major producing regions.

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor competition
frictionVectors.details: Control of Port Sudan and Nile-linked corridors has become central to military logistics and external diplomacy. Gulf, Russian, Egyptian, and other foreign interests seek influence over access without a stable national authority able to enforce terms.

highlights: Mining and gas bargaining power is rising

frictionVectors.title: Resource-contract pressure
frictionVectors.details: The government is seeking greater local participation and revenue capture in gold, critical minerals, and natural gas projects. Negotiations with multinational firms remain sensitive as Tanzania balances investment needs against sovereignty concerns.

frictionVectors.title: Port and rail competition
frictionVectors.details: The expansion of Dar es Salaam-linked rail and port corridors is drawing competition among Gulf, Chinese, Indian, and Western investors. Infrastructure dependence could improve bargaining power but also create new external leverage over trade routes.

highlights: Lomé remains a regional logistics hub

frictionVectors.title: Port dependency and foreign capital
frictionVectors.details: Lomé’s role as a transshipment and regional trade hub depends heavily on foreign shipping, logistics, and finance networks. This generates revenue but leaves strategic infrastructure exposed to external commercial influence.

frictionVectors.title: Phosphate-sector governance
frictionVectors.details: Phosphates remain a core national resource, yet aging infrastructure and limited downstream processing constrain domestic value capture. External buyers and investors retain substantial leverage over production modernization and export earnings.

frictionVectors.title: Migration and financing dependence
frictionVectors.details: The EU uses migration cooperation and budget support as major leverage while Tunisia resists externally imposed political and economic conditions. Stalled or limited IMF engagement leaves the country reliant on bilateral and European financing.

frictionVectors.title: Energy and phosphate vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: High energy-import dependence and underperforming phosphate production constrain sovereign economic control. Foreign investment is needed for infrastructure, but fiscal weakness limits Tunisia's bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: EACOP financing and sanctions pressure
frictionVectors.details: The China-backed, TotalEnergies-linked oil pipeline remains central to Uganda's export strategy but faces Western political, legal, and financial pressure over environmental and human-rights concerns. Delays could increase dependence on external financiers and transit partners.

frictionVectors.title: Regional export dependence
frictionVectors.details: Uganda's future oil revenues depend on Tanzanian infrastructure and regional security, limiting unilateral control over the value chain. The government is seeking greater local-content participation while retaining foreign technical and capital support.

frictionVectors.title: Mining ownership and contract pressure
frictionVectors.details: Copper prices and new investment improve Zambia's bargaining position, but foreign operators, especially Chinese and Western firms, retain substantial influence over production and processing. Lusaka faces pressure to secure higher state participation without deterring capital.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring has expanded fiscal space but continues to constrain independent spending and industrial policy. Rail, power, and logistics bottlenecks leave copper exports dependent on external infrastructure and regional corridors.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-mineral bargaining gap
frictionVectors.details: Zimbabwe has tightened controls on unprocessed lithium exports and seeks domestic beneficiation, but Chinese firms remain deeply embedded in mining, processing, and project finance. Limited access to Western capital weakens Harare's negotiating alternatives.

frictionVectors.title: Currency and sanctions constraints
frictionVectors.details: Currency instability, sanctions, and weak financial institutions reduce the state's ability to capture and reinvest resource rents. Gold, platinum, and lithium revenues remain vulnerable to leakage, informal trade, and opaque contracting.
